utterances.speaker: JUDGE BONOMY
utterances.text: Good morning, Mr. Riedlmayer.

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: Good morning, Your Honour.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE BONOMY
utterances.text: Your evidence will again continue. Mr. Hannis.

utterances.speaker: MR. HANNIS
utterances.text: Thank you, Your Honour.

utterances.speaker: MR. HANNIS
utterances.text: Good morning, Mr. Riedlmayer. Yesterday Mr. Bakrac asked you at page 5538, line 23, of the transcript, if it were "possible for a serious assessment of damage to be made on the basis of photos alone." And your answer was --

utterances.speaker: ANDRAS JANOS RIEDLMAYER [Resumed]
utterances.text: My answer was that it is indeed possible.

utterances.speaker: MR. HANNIS
utterances.text: And in the context of your report, you're basically just assigning one of five categories to the level of damage?

utterances.speaker: ANDRAS JANOS RIEDLMAYER [Resumed]
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: MR. HANNIS
utterances.text: Particularly in those cases where you were called upon to make an assessment based on photographs alone, in what way would you resolve a close question?

utterances.speaker: ANDRAS JANOS RIEDLMAYER [Resumed]
utterances.text: As I indicated in my testimony earlier, we were always extremely conservative in our assessments. So if there was any doubt, we would rule for the lesser damage.

utterances.speaker: MR. HANNIS
utterances.text: Even though it might appear -- it could be possibly classified as heavily damaged, you would rule it as lightly damaged, if all you had was the photograph?

utterances.speaker: ANDRAS JANOS RIEDLMAYER [Resumed]
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: MR. HANNIS
utterances.text: Regarding your ability to distinguish the types and possible causes of damage, for example, whether or not the damage had been caused by explosives placed in the interior or by firing from projectiles from the outside or bombing from the air, both Mr. Bakrac and Mr. Ivetic asked you some questions about your experience and abilities in that regard. You indicated that in the course of this project you got some on-the-job training so to speak.

utterances.speaker: ANDRAS JANOS RIEDLMAYER [Resumed]
utterances.text: That's correct.

utterances.speaker: MR. HANNIS
utterances.text: And did you learn anything in this regard from your partner, Mr. Herscher, who was an architect?

utterances.speaker: ANDRAS JANOS RIEDLMAYER [Resumed]
utterances.text: Yes. He knows something about the structure of buildings, and he had also worked in Bosnia after 1995, working on the restoration of buildings in Mostar.

utterances.speaker: MR. HANNIS
utterances.text: And in your answers to Mr. Bakrac at page 5539 and Mr. Ivetic, I believe, at page 5602, you mentioned that you had done a good -- you had read a good deal of the technical literature in this area.

utterances.speaker: ANDRAS JANOS RIEDLMAYER [Resumed]
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: MR. HANNIS
utterances.text: Can you explain or elaborate on that a little bit. What kinds of things were you reading?

utterances.speaker: ANDRAS JANOS RIEDLMAYER [Resumed]
utterances.text: There is a growing field of literature dealing with damage to heritage buildings in armed conflict. Publications such as by the observatory for the protection of cultural heritage in armed conflict at the University of Naples has a series of publications on this. The international committee on monuments and sites, a non-governmental organisation, has also had a series of publications, again with chapters that discuss the various types of damage, the various remedies for it and so forth. Quite aside from that, much of this is common sense if, for example, the rubble -- there's a hole in the building, the rubble is inside the building, I think it's usually safe to assume that the force that caused the hole came from outside the building. Similarly, if the rubble is scattered at some distance from the building, if there are radiating cracks from where the hole is and soot marks radiating outward from the site of the damage, it is often safe to assume that the explosive was inside the structure.

utterances.speaker: MR. HANNIS
utterances.text: Thank you. At page 5553, line 24 through 5555 at line 9, Mr. Bakrac was asking you about your description of the damage at the old bazaar Peje/Pec, and the source of your information for the allegation that the damage you saw was a result of having been burnt down by Serb police in June of 1999. First of all, in your answer at line 14 on page 5555, you indicated that several individuals told you this and that they barraged you with this information.

utterances.speaker: ANDRAS JANOS RIEDLMAYER [Resumed]
utterances.text: That's correct.

utterances.speaker: MR. HANNIS
utterances.text: When did you visit that site?

utterances.speaker: ANDRAS JANOS RIEDLMAYER [Resumed]
utterances.text: In October of 1999.

utterances.speaker: MR. HANNIS
utterances.text: Okay. And you personally have no way of knowing who the perpetrators are?

utterances.speaker: ANDRAS JANOS RIEDLMAYER [Resumed]
utterances.text: I was not there earlier, no.

utterances.speaker: MR. HANNIS
utterances.text: However, based on what you observed at that time, was the damage consistent with having been burned down from the ground up?

utterances.speaker: ANDRAS JANOS RIEDLMAYER [Resumed]
utterances.text: Yes. I based that on several signs that I saw. First of all, the entire line of shops had been obliterated, basically. The rubble was, in all cases, pushed to the back of the site, and it was heavily charred. What was also significant, in my view, is that there was no damage to the next row of buildings in from the street on the side street behind. So it was limited to the shop fronts facing the street.

utterances.speaker: MR. HANNIS
utterances.text: Was it consistent or inconsistent with an allegation of it having been caused by NATO bombing?

utterances.speaker: ANDRAS JANOS RIEDLMAYER [Resumed]
utterances.text: I would judge that to be inconsistent with an allegation that it done from the air.

utterances.speaker: MR. HANNIS
utterances.text: Was it consistent or inconsistent with the allegation that it had occurred in June of 1999?

utterances.speaker: ANDRAS JANOS RIEDLMAYER [Resumed]
utterances.text: Well, the damage looked relatively fresh as of October. I have no way of judging whether it happened in May or June, but I would say it's safe that it didn't happen six months earlier.

utterances.speaker: MR. HANNIS
utterances.text: All right. Yesterday, at page 5571, Judge Bonomy asked you a question about the indictment that you had seen prior to writing your report in 2001. Do you recall, did that indictment have any -- list any specific sites or locations with regard to cultural damage?

utterances.speaker: ANDRAS JANOS RIEDLMAYER [Resumed]
utterances.text: No. That version of the indictment, as far as I recall, did not have a schedule of sites under the rubric of cultural heritage. There were sites mentioned that had to do with other charges.

utterances.speaker: MR. HANNIS
utterances.text: With regard to cultural heritage, was it just a general allegation?

utterances.speaker: ANDRAS JANOS RIEDLMAYER [Resumed]
utterances.text: A general allegation in the first indictment, yes.

utterances.speaker: MR. HANNIS
utterances.text: Okay. Now I want to move on to some of the questions Mr. Fila asked you --

utterances.speaker: JUDGE BONOMY
utterances.text: Well, the evidence there is that there were sites mentioned in other charges, although there wasn't a charge relating to damage to cultural heritage. Let's be sure we're not at cross-purposes.

utterances.speaker: MR. HANNIS
utterances.text: No, Your Honour, there were other sites mentioned with regard to deportations or killings.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE BONOMY
utterances.text: Thank you.

utterances.speaker: MR. HANNIS
utterances.text: Thank you.

utterances.speaker: MR. HANNIS
utterances.text: At page 5582, line 23, Mr. Fila told you how he had or has the impression that you -- that you wrapped up your research quickly and he thought that -- that that quick wrapping up had something to do with "something to do with the arrest of Mr. Milosevic." Did it?

utterances.speaker: ANDRAS JANOS RIEDLMAYER [Resumed]
utterances.text: No. Our research took us over two years, and the arrest of Milosevic came towards the end of that two years.

utterances.speaker: MR. HANNIS
utterances.text: Mr. Fila also said he thought "you were receiving instructions from the Prosecutor to wrap things up as quickly as possible so the indictment can be supplemented." Any truth to that suspicion on Mr. Fila's part?

utterances.speaker: ANDRAS JANOS RIEDLMAYER [Resumed]
utterances.text: I wasn't under pressure from the Prosecutor, but we were told that any data we wanted to submit had to be in by the autumn of 2001.

utterances.speaker: MR. HANNIS
utterances.text: And who told you that?

utterances.speaker: ANDRAS JANOS RIEDLMAYER [Resumed]
utterances.text: That was the Office of the Prosecutor.

utterances.speaker: MR. HANNIS
utterances.text: Okay. Page 5586, line 16, Mr. Fila asked you about whether you had gone to Belgrade to try to get additional information relative to the White Book and allegations about NATO damage to Serb cultural sites. First of all, I want to confirm, was the White Book your only source of information about such damage?

utterances.speaker: ANDRAS JANOS RIEDLMAYER [Resumed]
utterances.text: It was not the only source.

utterances.speaker: MR. HANNIS
utterances.text: Was it your primary source?

utterances.speaker: ANDRAS JANOS RIEDLMAYER [Resumed]
utterances.text: No. It was one of several sources.

utterances.speaker: MR. HANNIS
utterances.text: Okay. Now, regarding Gracanica -- well, actually, let's --

utterances.speaker: MR. HANNIS
utterances.text: I would like to pull up an exhibit now, Exhibit P2472.

utterances.speaker: MR. HANNIS
utterances.text: We have a couple of extracts from the White Book. Do you have that on your screen? Do you recognise that.

utterances.speaker: ANDRAS JANOS RIEDLMAYER [Resumed]
utterances.text: It hasn't come up yet.

utterances.speaker: MR. HANNIS
utterances.text: And you recognise the cover page?

utterances.speaker: ANDRAS JANOS RIEDLMAYER [Resumed]
utterances.text: That is the title page, yes.

utterances.speaker: MR. HANNIS
utterances.text: If we could go to the next page of this exhibit. And if we could scroll down to the bottom of the page.

utterances.speaker: MR. HANNIS
utterances.text: Mr. Riedlmayer, can you see a reference to Gracanica --

utterances.speaker: ANDRAS JANOS RIEDLMAYER [Resumed]
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: MR. HANNIS
utterances.text: -- at page 226?

utterances.speaker: ANDRAS JANOS RIEDLMAYER [Resumed]
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: MR. HANNIS
utterances.text: Can you read what was in the White Book about Gracanica?

utterances.speaker: ANDRAS JANOS RIEDLMAYER [Resumed]
utterances.text: It says: "The Church of the Assumption in the Gracanica Monastery, the endowment of King Milutin, was built in the second decade of the 14th century. The monastery keeps a significant collection of icons" and other descriptions of the monastery. "On the night of 30/31 March, the village of Gracanica was bombed for the third time, while four shells fell 500 metres away from the Gracanica monastery. With continuous, unrelenting bombardment of Pristina, Gracanica is further endangered by detonations."

utterances.speaker: MR. HANNIS
utterances.text: Could we go to the next page of this exhibit and if we could, yes, focus in on the top.

utterances.speaker: MR. HANNIS
utterances.text: Regarding Pec and the Patriarch of Pec could you read that?

utterances.speaker: ANDRAS JANOS RIEDLMAYER [Resumed]
utterances.text: Yes. "The Patriarchate of Pec: The complex of the Pec churches is the spiritual seat and mausoleum of Serbian archbishops and patriarchs, built in the third decade of the 13th century. During the bombardment on the night of 31 March/1 April, the pumping station of the city water-supply system, situated 500 metres from the monastery of the Patriarchate of Pec, was struck. The old city centre was bombed during day-time on 10 April, and after a series of repeated bombings of Pec, on the night of 14/15 April the old city centre was heavily damaged."

utterances.speaker: THE INTERPRETER
utterances.text: Kindly slow down for the interpreters, please.

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: I'm sorry.

utterances.speaker: MR. HANNIS
utterances.text: That's okay. If we could go to the next page. Yes, we have another entry in volume 2. If we go to the following page, the last page in this that is marked Gracanica.

utterances.speaker: MR. HANNIS
utterances.text: Could you read that one for us.

utterances.speaker: ANDRAS JANOS RIEDLMAYER [Resumed]
utterances.text: "Gracanica: The village Gracanica has been the target of countless attacks since the beginning of the war. It was once again targeted again on the 1st of May. The missiles landed about 500 metres from the monastery, causing the loosening of the walls."

utterances.speaker: MR. HANNIS
utterances.text: Now, in your report you indicated that in addition to the White Book you had other sources from Serb authorities or Serb websites?

utterances.speaker: ANDRAS JANOS RIEDLMAYER [Resumed]
utterances.text: I'm thinking, for example, the Ministry of Information website in Belgrade which issued repeated statements on these matters including statements about Gracanica and Pec.

utterances.speaker: MR. HANNIS
utterances.text: If we could go next to Exhibit 2471.

utterances.speaker: MR. HANNIS
utterances.text: And I think you have a full list of those other sources in your report at footnotes 9 to 11?

utterances.speaker: ANDRAS JANOS RIEDLMAYER [Resumed]
utterances.text: That's correct.

utterances.speaker: MR. HANNIS
utterances.text: Okay. I would like, with the assistance of the usher, if I could hand you a hard copy of the document that's on the screen. And if I could have you read the highlighted portions of that that are pertinent to this discussion at that moment.

utterances.speaker: ANDRAS JANOS RIEDLMAYER [Resumed]
utterances.text: Yes. This comes from the Serbian government website maintained by the Ministry of Information. It is dispatched by the state news agency Tanjug on June 12th, 1999. "During the two and a half month barbaric bombing of Yugoslavia, some 160 cultural monuments in Serbia have been most seriously endangered, damaged or destroyed ..." "According to the information of the Institute for the Protection of the Cultural Monuments of Serbia, stated today ... by the institute's collaborator, Svetlana Pejic ..." "Through direct hits of the NATO air force, 24 monuments ... have been destroyed, through actions in close proximity, 78 have been damaged and, due to detonations, 57 cultural monuments have been endangered ..." "The old city centres of Djakovica and Pec ... have been irreparably destroyed." "Among the 13 damaged monasteries and 11 churches, Gracanica" --

utterances.speaker: MR. HANNIS
utterances.text: I'm sorry, Your Honour. Mr. Fila is standing up.

utterances.speaker: MR. FILA
utterances.text: [Microphone not activated]

utterances.speaker: THE INTERPRETER
utterances.text: Microphone, please, for Mr. Fila.

utterances.speaker: MR. FILA
utterances.text: [Interpretation] The interpreters are telling us, as you all speak English, of course it's fast enough for you, but they don't have time to interpret into Serbian. It's not an objection, it's just for the sake of interpretation.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE BONOMY
utterances.text: Thank you, Mr. Fila, for drawing that approximate to our attention. It was remiss of me not to be wearing the headphones. If you could both slow down a little and also observe a pause between question and answer that would help the interpreters greatly.

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: Should I repeat anything?

utterances.speaker: JUDGE BONOMY
utterances.text: I think we all have the document on the screen, but just continue your reading more slowly.

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: Thank you, Your Honour.

utterances.speaker: MR. HANNIS
utterances.text: And I think if we could scroll to the next page of the document he's about to read from.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE BONOMY
utterances.text: Just before you continue reading, is this item footnoted in the report?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: It is. It's --

utterances.speaker: MR. HANNIS
utterances.text: That's footnote 9, Your Honour, I believe.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE BONOMY
utterances.text: Footnote 9. Thank you.

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: So: "Among the 13 damaged monasteries and the 11 churches, Gracanica has suffered the greatest amount of damage. "Due to the explosions of several dozens of missiles in the close proximity ... the facade of the church has been damaged and numerous creaks have appeared in the fresco paintings, widening after every detonation. Parts of the frescoes have been broken off walls. The damage done to the building of the old, eastern bedrooms of the Gracanica monastery, the frescoes of which are in all the encyclopaedias of the world, is visible. "The Pec Patriarchate has been several damaged also ... old creaks in the frescoes have widened and new have appeared. Parts of frescoes have been broken off walls." And I believe that is the end of the excerpts.

utterances.speaker: MR. HANNIS
utterances.text: I assume there the reference to creeks probably means cracks?

utterances.speaker: ANDRAS JANOS RIEDLMAYER [Resumed]
utterances.text: That's right.

utterances.speaker: MR. HANNIS
utterances.text: Now, did you visit Gracanica personally?

utterances.speaker: ANDRAS JANOS RIEDLMAYER [Resumed]
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: MR. HANNIS
utterances.text: What did you see there in terms of damage, compared to what's described in the White Book and this website?

utterances.speaker: ANDRAS JANOS RIEDLMAYER [Resumed]
utterances.text: I could see no sign of recent damage. Much of the monastery has been heavily restored over the years, so there are old blasted-over cracks. When touching the walls, you could also feel the dampness rising up from the ground. More specifically, conservators who have visited the site subsequently, have reported -- and these are conservators who have expertise in mural paintings -- have reported that there is no damage other than that from the rising damp and deferred maintenance.

utterances.speaker: MR. HANNIS
utterances.text: And you didn't see any evidence that would be consistent with damage from NATO bombing?

utterances.speaker: ANDRAS JANOS RIEDLMAYER [Resumed]
utterances.text: No, I did not.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE BONOMY
utterances.text: When you went there, were you in possession of this article?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: Yes, I was. That's one of the reasons I went there, Your Honour.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE BONOMY
utterances.text: Now, there are two possibilities here. One is that these various features highlighted, in other words, parts of frescoes broken off walls, damage to the building of the old eastern bedrooms, is possible that that damage did exist. Can you say whether that's right? And then the second question is: Whether, if it did exist, it was consistent with bombing, the result of a bomb blast.

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: Well, I saw no signs of the damage, Your Honour --

utterances.speaker: JUDGE BONOMY
utterances.text: So you're saying this is misleading in its description of the state of the building?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: As far as my observations and those of other professionals who have visited the site are concerned.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE BONOMY
utterances.text: Who are these other professionals?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: In the case of the Pec Patriarchate, a team from the Italian Instituto Centrale di Rettorato, the central institute for restoration, did a project on the Pec Patriarchate in the aftermath of the war. They published an entire monograph on it. And subsequently, in collaboration with an organisation of Serb conservation professionals, issued a report on damaged and endangered heritage in Kosovo. And their conclusions state in so many words that all damage observed had to do with deferred maintenance and problems of rising ground-water.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE BONOMY
utterances.text: That's a separate question, I think, Mr. Riedlmayer. My first point to you is whether this damage actually exists.

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: I think in terms of -- of cracks, there are old cracks. And I had no way of judging whether the cracks were, you know, millimetres wider than they had been before.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE BONOMY
utterances.text: But, you see, that's -- I thought you had said initially, just now, that this was misleading. For example, "parts of frescoes have been broken off walls."

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: I saw no sign of that having occurred, and I also asked the monks, who were escorting us, to show me if there had been any damage during the war, and they were not able to show me any.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE BONOMY
utterances.text: Well, I'm thinking of damage that might even pre-exist the war. You know, the two separate questions are: What is the state of the building? And separately: How much of it can be attributed, if any, to the bombing? And I'm trying to focus for the moment what was the state of the building. Is this an accurate description?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: No, it's not I don't know. It is a building that is almost 700 years old, and therefore it has had many ravages of time and repairs done to it. There was an extensive restoration of the building before the war, but the building hasn't been kept up for more than a decade since then.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE BONOMY
utterances.text: All right. Thank you.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE CHOWHAN
utterances.text: Excuse me, did you check when was the last restoration carried on. And from taking that as a benchmark or as a measurement of time, were you then able to see any cracks or fissures coming up after the restoration? Were you able to check this with respect to the restoration after?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: Well, I did not, Your Honour, I did not have the detailed documentation in hand when I visited the site. However, I have seen three books that talk about that restoration and have extensive photographs of the most important parts of the monastery. And what I saw is consistent with what I saw in those three books, and those photographs all pre-date the war. So I am convinced that there was no additional damage caused by the war. There is an ongoing issue of, you know, the gradual dilapidation of an old building. For example, if a building built of brick doesn't have the mortar pointed at regular intervals, the mortar tends to crumble and fall out which allows rain and other things to fall inwards, which in the long term does raise issues. But, no, there was no visible damage.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE CHOWHAN
utterances.text: You actually saw those restorations? Did somebody point out the restoration? And then standing over there, did you see any damage caused because -- or not caused?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: The restorations are very evident, Your Honour, because there are broad white streaks where plaster has been put over old cracks, but that is -- it was clearly not recent. It dated from the pre-war restorations.

utterances.speaker: MR. HANNIS
utterances.text: Thank you. You've already been talking now about what I wanted to show you next, Exhibit P2470, I believe, I'd like to put up now. And this relates to another web site. I believe this is the one that is YU Heritage. Is that a site that you visited before you went to Kosovo?

utterances.speaker: ANDRAS JANOS RIEDLMAYER [Resumed]
utterances.text: Yes, and it's cited in my -- in the notes to my report.

utterances.speaker: MR. HANNIS
utterances.text: Okay. And can you -- can you read that first description regarding the Patriarchate of Pec.

utterances.speaker: ANDRAS JANOS RIEDLMAYER [Resumed]
utterances.text: "The Patriarchate of Pec. NATO bombs repeatedly detonated in the nearest vicinity. Due to detonations the walls of the churches are badly shaken. The old fissures on the fresco paintings have widened and new ones appeared. Portions of the frescoes have detached from the walls and their collapse is imminent."

utterances.speaker: MR. HANNIS
utterances.text: Now, could we go to the next page.

utterances.speaker: MR. HANNIS
utterances.text: Did you actually visit this site?

utterances.speaker: ANDRAS JANOS RIEDLMAYER [Resumed]
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: MR. HANNIS
utterances.text: And to the --

utterances.speaker: MR. HANNIS
utterances.text: Am I too fast again?

utterances.speaker: MR. FILA
utterances.text: [Interpretation] No, not this time, but could you please explain where this document is from. I don't know what you're reading. What is the provenance of the document.

utterances.speaker: MR. HANNIS
utterances.text: Mr. Riedlmayer, can you answer that, please?

utterances.speaker: ANDRAS JANOS RIEDLMAYER [Resumed]
utterances.text: Yes. This is from a web site put up by the Institute for the Protection of Monuments of the Republic of Serbia.

utterances.speaker: MR. HANNIS
utterances.text: If we could go to the next page.

utterances.speaker: MR. FILA
utterances.text: [Interpretation] And where is this in your list?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: It is in the footnotes to my report between footnotes 9 and 11.

utterances.speaker: MR. HANNIS
utterances.text: I believe this one is also in footnote 9. And can we go to the next page, please. And finally the last page I think is the one I want.

utterances.speaker: MR. HANNIS
utterances.text: Mr. Riedlmayer, is this church a part of the complex?

utterances.speaker: ANDRAS JANOS RIEDLMAYER [Resumed]
utterances.text: It is part of the complex, yes.

utterances.speaker: MR. HANNIS
utterances.text: And this appears to show some cracks in frescoes and the photos are purported to be April/May 1999. Did you see those cracks when you there?

utterances.speaker: ANDRAS JANOS RIEDLMAYER [Resumed]
utterances.text: I did see the cracks; however, I looked at pre-war photographs that also showed the same cracks.

utterances.speaker: MR. HANNIS
utterances.text: Okay.

utterances.speaker: ANDRAS JANOS RIEDLMAYER [Resumed]
utterances.text: And the Italian study discusses them at some length.

utterances.speaker: MR. HANNIS
utterances.text: And concludes what about --

utterances.speaker: ANDRAS JANOS RIEDLMAYER [Resumed]
utterances.text: And concludes that it is caused by natural factors.

utterances.speaker: MR. HANNIS
utterances.text: Okay. All right. Now I want to move on to another topic. Mr. Ivetic in his cross-examination --

utterances.speaker: JUDGE BONOMY
utterances.text: Well, just before you --

utterances.speaker: MR. HANNIS
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE BONOMY
utterances.text: -- do. The pre-war photographs that you refer to, is any of them in the database?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: They are not in the database, sir. I was not allowed to take pictures inside of Gracanica and Pec because of the KFOR troops that were stationed outside, prohibiting photography.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE BONOMY
utterances.text: Thank you. Mr. Hannis.

utterances.speaker: MR. HANNIS
utterances.text: But your reference to pre-war photographs --

utterances.speaker: MR. ACKERMAN
utterances.text: Excuse me.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE BONOMY
utterances.text: Mr. Ackerman, I think.

utterances.speaker: MR. ACKERMAN
utterances.text: Your Honour, I think the witness didn't answer your question. You asked him about pre-war photographs and he said he wasn't allowed to take any photographs. That doesn't deal with pre-war photographs; that deals with post-war.

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: Oh, I'm sorry. The pre-war photographs I referred to were in works, such as Gojko Subotic's book, Kosovo, Art of the Sacred Land, and a number of other monographs on Serbian Orthodox heritage of Kosovo, which shows the interiors of these churches.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE BONOMY
utterances.text: But they're not in the database?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: They're not in the database.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE BONOMY
utterances.text: Mr. Fila, did you have a point to make?

utterances.speaker: MR. FILA
utterances.text: [Interpretation] I wanted to say the same thing Mr. Ackerman did. I didn't understand one thing, though. Perhaps it may sound like an unusual question, but this is some new data. As for the findings of the Italian conservators and the Serbian conservators, is that among the data provided by Mr. Riedlmayer? We have an assertion here that these fissures date from an earlier point in time, then we have them mentioned in the Italian report and in the Serbian report, but I don't see this among the material that we received.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE BONOMY
utterances.text: It's not -- it is not in the material presented to the Court, but this is a matter, of course, that you have ample time to explore further later when you present your own case.

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: Can I, Your Honour?

utterances.speaker: JUDGE BONOMY
utterances.text: Mr. Riedlmayer.

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: I would like to point out that my report to the Tribunal in this matter was submitted in 2001. The joint report of the Italian and Serbian conservators was published in 2003, as was the monograph by the Italian Institute for Restoration. If the Court so wishes, I can provide the references.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE BONOMY
utterances.text: Well, I think that would be of assistance to at least Defence counsel, if you can. Do you have that available or is that --

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: Not on me, but I can provide it.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE BONOMY
utterances.text: You should provide it through the Office of the Prosecutor, who will relay it to Defence counsel.

utterances.speaker: MR. HANNIS
utterances.text: I will. Thank you, Your Honour.

utterances.speaker: MR. HANNIS
utterances.text: Mr. Riedlmayer, I wanted to move on to a question that Mr. Ivetic asked you at page 5605, line 9 and following, and this will help me, too. Can you distinguish for me the deference between a kulla and a family compound. Are all kullas family compounds or are all family compounds kullas? What's the difference?

utterances.speaker: ANDRAS JANOS RIEDLMAYER [Resumed]
utterances.text: The answer to both of your questions is, no, in short. A kulla is a very particular kind of stone building, traditionally built by Albanians in Kosovo and in adjacent areas -- Albanian-inhabited areas of the districts of Plav and Gusinje, Montenegro. That's G-u-s-i-n-j-e. And a family compound is simply a group of buildings, whether modern or of the kulla type, that houses various branches of an extended family. What I was simply referring to is that many kullas are located in such compounds, but not all such compounds consist of kullas.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE BONOMY
utterances.text: Mr. Riedlmayer, are kullas also tradition to Albania itself?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: They are found in small numbers in northern Albania, but many of them were destroyed during the Enver Hoxha regime.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE BONOMY
utterances.text: Mr. Hannis.

utterances.speaker: MR. HANNIS
utterances.text: I guess it's me. I'm still not fully clear. If I have a family compound consisting of several buildings that are connected and surrounded by walls and the lower part of each of the houses is built of stone, is that a kulla?

utterances.speaker: ANDRAS JANOS RIEDLMAYER [Resumed]
utterances.text: A kulla is more than just a building of which the lower part is built of stone. The entire building is monumental, it's usually two, sometimes three storeys high. The top storey is usually elaborately finished. It's usually at the corner of the building and it is known as the guest-room, which is where major occasions, family occasions take place. It is easily distinguishable from any other kind of house.

utterances.speaker: MR. HANNIS
utterances.text: Okay. And then finally there's just a vocabulary item I want to clear up with you in the transcript, if I can find the reference. I think the first one at is at page 5597 from yesterday. And you were discussing with Mr. Ivetic kullas and whether or not they were -- could be used as defensive structures. And your answer -- you described how someone had reported to you fleeing and seeing the kulla destroyed by a hand-held device firing a flammable into it. You say: "So in a -- it's transcribed so in a lead-out in late 20th century warfare they had absolutely no utility." I thought I heard you say "redoubt."

utterances.speaker: ANDRAS JANOS RIEDLMAYER [Resumed]
utterances.text: Neither. I have -- oh, as a redoubt.

utterances.speaker: MR. HANNIS
utterances.text: And on page 5598, you also said that they would make very poor lead-outs, I assume again that was redoubts in the sense of a fortification of some kind?

utterances.speaker: ANDRAS JANOS RIEDLMAYER [Resumed]
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE BONOMY
utterances.text: I don't think we got the spelling right yet. Mr. Riedlmayer, I think it should be r-e-d-o-u-b-t. It's obviously a word with which the transcribers are not familiar, but it was used several times in yesterday's evidence.

utterances.speaker: MR. HANNIS
utterances.text: Those were the two that I had noted yesterday when I was taking notes. If there are more, I would propose that we make those corrections as well.

utterances.speaker: THE INTERPRETER
utterances.text: Would the speakers please pause between questions and answers. The interpreters cannot follow you.

utterances.speaker: MR. HANNIS
utterances.text: Thank you. I'll try to slow down, and actually I'll stop. I have no more questions.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE BONOMY
utterances.text: Mr. Bakrac.

utterances.speaker: MR. BAKRAC
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Your Honour, I believe we are entitled to put some additional questions, and I may have only a couple.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE BONOMY
utterances.text: In respect of what, Mr. Bakrac?

utterances.speaker: MR. BAKRAC
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Regarding Gracanica and some additional information we have concerning the restoration works and fissures, and there is another piece of information concerning Mr. Riedlmayer's findings in those places he actually did not visit but rather made his conclusions based on photographs. So these are the only two questions I have.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE BONOMY
utterances.text: Well, the second matter has been explored adequately, has it not? What do you want to raise in relation to the photographs and the use of photographs as a tool in assessing damage?

utterances.speaker: MR. BAKRAC
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Your Honour, we heard today that the damage, or rather, the assessment of the damage based on photographs, as said by himself, by the witness, were incorrect. They were made to appear less significant than the actual damage. I believe this was at the very outset of the re-direct today.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE BONOMY
utterances.text: All he said was he gave the benefit of the doubt by choosing the lesser rather than the higher form of damage, if there was any doubt in his mind about which it was. You want to challenge that, do you?

utterances.speaker: MR. BAKRAC
utterances.text: [Interpretation] No, Your Honour. I wanted to ask this: Whether this was done precisely because a photograph can not be considered a reliable source to assess any type of damage.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE BONOMY
utterances.text: You've had adequate opportunity to explore the issue of the use of photographs as a tool for evaluation of damage, but I will allow you to ask further questions about Gracanica in view of the more detailed exploration of the matter that has been carried out in the re-examination.

utterances.speaker: MR. BAKRAC
utterances.text: [Interpretation] I have only one question regarding that.

utterances.speaker: MR. BAKRAC
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Mr. Riedlmayer, you told us just now that you examined Gracanica personally. Is that correct?

utterances.speaker: ANDRAS JANOS RIEDLMAYER [Resumed]
utterances.text: That's correct.

utterances.speaker: MR. BAKRAC
utterances.text: It's also correct, I assume, that once you carried out that examination, you saw cracks in the walls. Is that correct?

utterances.speaker: ANDRAS JANOS RIEDLMAYER [Resumed]
utterances.text: I saw old -- what appeared to be old plastered-over cracks.

utterances.speaker: MR. BAKRAC
utterances.text: Can you assess the age of the cracks, how old are they?

utterances.speaker: ANDRAS JANOS RIEDLMAYER [Resumed]
utterances.text: All I can say is that the plaster did not appear to be fresh. It had a patina of dirt on it. So I assume that it had not been applied in the immediate recent past. As you know, churches have candles and other activities in them that generate some amount of smoke and other particles, which then settle on the walls.

utterances.speaker: MR. BAKRAC
utterances.text: Did you have any pre-war photographs, such as in other cases where you carried out assessments? Did you have pre-war photographs of these places so as to be able to compare? When I say "these places," I mean the parts on which you spotted cracks.

utterances.speaker: ANDRAS JANOS RIEDLMAYER [Resumed]
utterances.text: Yes. Some of the books I mentioned which were published in the late 1990s, just before the war, and thus I assume showed the state of the buildings immediately prior to the war. I'm referring to books like Mr. Subotic's book on the Art of Kosovo.

utterances.speaker: MR. BAKRAC
utterances.text: In that book, specifically concerning Gracanica, did you notice a pre-war photograph depicting details of the cracks you subsequently saw when you carried out your personal check-up of the place, so as to be able to compare?

utterances.speaker: ANDRAS JANOS RIEDLMAYER [Resumed]
utterances.text: I saw the photographs of the interior. They showed the same plastered-over cracks that I saw during my visit. What I was telling the Court earlier is that I was not able to take comparative photographs myself because photography was not permitted. But what I saw during my visit corresponded to what I had seen in Mr. Subotic's book.

utterances.speaker: MR. BAKRAC
utterances.text: Therefore, you claim that what you saw in Mr. Subotic's book compared to the cracks, that they -- that the book shows the very same cracks you saw there?

utterances.speaker: ANDRAS JANOS RIEDLMAYER [Resumed]
utterances.text: That is my conclusion, yes.

utterances.speaker: MR. BAKRAC
utterances.text: Thank you, Mr. Riedlmayer. I have no more questions.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE CHOWHAN
utterances.text: Well, there's one Byzantinian monument on the St. Sofia which has been adopted by plural religions to be a worship place and it still exists, mosque and the church. Now, would this and the question Mr. Bakrac had asked earlier, whether the people respected the Ottoman heritage as their heritage, did you spot any such places in Sofia in your sojourn to this area and where you found in respect of both coming up and whether such monuments or a monument was kept intact or destroyed by any of the ethnic groups? I'm grateful.

utterances.speaker: ANDRAS JANOS RIEDLMAYER [Resumed]
utterances.text: Your question is a little hard to answer because there is nothing quite the equivalent in Kosovo to Ija Sofia which at various points was a church, then a mosque, and now a museum. The closest, perhaps, is the church of the Virgini Leviska in Prizren, which was built in the last century before the Ottoman conquest. After the Ottoman conquest, as the principal cathedral church in town, it was converted into a mosque. And then following the conquest of Kosovo by the Serbian kingdom in 1912, it was turned back into a church and is a World Heritage Site. At the time I visited in 1999, it had not been touched, either by the NATO bombing or by the local Albanians. Subsequently in 2004, there were riots and it suffered damage, unfortunately. There were many places in Kosovo that were revered by both Muslim Albanians and by Serbs, and I think part of the tragedy of the events of 1998/1999 is that this kind of co-existence was shattered and may not be possible for a long time again.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE CHOWHAN
utterances.text: Thank you.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE BONOMY
utterances.text: Mr. Ivetic, do you wish now to complete your submissions?

utterances.speaker: MR. IVETIC
utterances.text: Sure, Your Honour. I don't know if we need the witness.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE BONOMY
utterances.text: No, I just want to be clear. That's what we can now proceed to do.

utterances.speaker: MR. IVETIC
utterances.text: Yes, yes.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE BONOMY
utterances.text: Well, Mr. Riedlmayer, that completes your evidence. Thank you for coming again to the Tribunal for giving it and for spending an extra day with us and you're now free to leave.

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: Thank you, Your Honour.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE BONOMY
utterances.text: Mr. Ivetic.

utterances.speaker: MR. IVETIC
utterances.text: Thank you, Your Honour. As I had previously advised the Court, and I think it's now clearer from the -- from having gone through all the various extracts from this study, is that there are a multitude of extracts that are not based upon anything that this witness saw that are based upon what he was told, particularly with respect to how damage occurred by other entities, including this Sabri Bajgora of the Islamic community and the IMG database, of which we don't know how the Bajgora group collected the information, whether they in fact based it upon interviews with persons, whether the persons they interviewed were eye-witnesses or not, et cetera. This is the same type of defective second- third- and fourth-hand information that Your Honours have previously stricken from the evidence. For the sake of clarity, according to my notes, the following exhibits are ones that are based entirely on this second-hand information from the Bajgora group and the IMG database with the caveat that, of course, we've heard that the IMG database has nothing about how damage occurred. So essentially, it boils down to information from the Bajgora group as to how damage occurred and that's Exhibits P1773, P1774, P1775, P1776, P1777, P1778 --

utterances.speaker: JUDGE BONOMY
utterances.text: I think you could speed this up by telling us between what numbers and going to the ones that are exceptional.

utterances.speaker: MR. IVETIC
utterances.text: Well, Your Honour, the next two are not on my list for the Bajgora group. The next two are ones that were apparently based only on news where there are no informant information listed for persons that may have been talked with and which Your Honours have already said you will not rely upon in great detail. It all boils down to the fact, as far as I understand it, the only sites where this witness visited and actually spoke with persons personally and recorded the persons he spoke with and what they said, the only ones that would not fall under the objection would be P1781, P1782, P1783 and I've got listed P1788 with a question mark. I think, from my recollection of the testimony, the witness was in Vucitrn municipality and in Djakovica municipality of the -- of the sites that are relevant to the indictment. And therefore I would submit that for the reasons that we have previously identified, namely the lack of probative value, the questions as to credibility and problems with accepting such second- and third-hand information from unknown sources as written evidence that goes towards the acts and conducts alleged against either the accused or alleged subordinates of the accused, violates the Rules of the Tribunal with respect to evidence and we would ask that those exhibits either be stricken in their entirety or, perhaps, be -- have the part that deals with how the damage was said to have occurred stricken or redacted. I think that would perhaps be the more conservative approach, and so that's why I give Your Honours both options and leave it for the Court to decide. And I think that's pretty much all I have on that score.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE BONOMY
utterances.text: Thank you, Mr. Ivetic. Mr. Hannis.

utterances.speaker: MR. HANNIS
utterances.text: Your Honour, we certainly object to the request that the exhibits in the entirety be stricken. I think that's throwing the baby out with the bath water. And I don't think it gives Your Honours enough credit to be able to assess little or no weight to that as hearsay. I make the argument I made earlier, I think it's premature to take that step until you've heard all the evidence in this case. And until you've heard all the evidence about a particular site or an event, those statements that Mr. Riedlmayer heard or recorded in his report should be available [Realtime transcript read in error "entitled"] to everybody. I see the transcript ends with me saying "available" to everybody, I meant to say "entitled."

utterances.speaker: JUDGE BONOMY
utterances.text: I had one other question about exhibits, Mr. Hannis. There is a CD of the IMG database, but that is not an exhibit. Is that correct?

utterances.speaker: MR. HANNIS
utterances.text: We had not tendered that, Your Honour. It is available from Mr. Riedlmayer.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE BONOMY
utterances.text: Well, we're satisfied that all of the exhibits challenged are admissible, and they are admissible in their entirety. Each one has relevance to Count 5, apart from certain other elements of other counts in the indictment. Parts of them may be given ultimately no weight at all. But even to understand the basis -- to properly understand the basis for the witness's conclusions, one has to have available all the information that he had. Indeed, it may be relevant to deciding to reject a conclusion that he has reached, that he based it on very weak hearsay, to which we would give no weight. So it would be an artificial exercise to pick our way through these exhibits and, as it were, fillet them of material which is of a particular type of hearsay. So we shall neither strike any of the exhibits or redact parts of them, but we will take a very cautious approach to the hearsay content of these when we come eventually to evaluate the various submissions made by the parties about the evidence of this witness. That takes us to the next witness, Mr. Hannis.

utterances.speaker: MR. HANNIS
utterances.text: Yes, Your Honour. Thank you. Before we move to him, I did want to indicate that of the book by Gojko Subotic, it is listed in the bibliography that appears in the Exhibit 1550, related to the patriarch. It is a book that was published in 1998 called, The Art of Kosovo. And that's for the benefit of the Defence counsel in the court.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE BONOMY
utterances.text: Thank you, Mr. Hannis.

utterances.speaker: MR. HANNIS
utterances.text: Ms. Moeller has the next witness.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE BONOMY
utterances.text: Ms. Moeller.

utterances.speaker: MS. MOELLER
utterances.text: The next witness, Your Honours, is Sabri Popaj, and he's taking us back to the municipality of Orahovac/Rahovec and specifically to the killing charge contained in paragraphs 75(b), Bela Crkva, Schedule B, but also paragraphs 72(a), 72(a)(i), 25 to 32, and the Prosecution charges in paragraphs 77(a), (b), and (d).

utterances.speaker: JUDGE BONOMY
utterances.text: Now, this witness is presented under Rule 92 ter. Is that correct?

utterances.speaker: MS. MOELLER
utterances.text: This witness was originally a live witness, but we decided to tender his statement and will lead just a short bit in live. He will be very helpful in pointing out the locations where the killings occurred on some photographs, mainly.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE BONOMY
utterances.text: Good morning, Mr. Popaj.

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Good morning.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE BONOMY
utterances.text: Would you please now make the solemn declaration to tell the truth by reading aloud the document which will now be placed before you.

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: [Interpretation] I solemnly declare that I will speak the truth, the whole truth, and nothing but the truth.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE BONOMY
utterances.text: Thank you. Please be seated. Mr. Popaj, we have before us a lengthy statement, which you gave to the Prosecution in June 1999, and we also have some corrections you made to it in the year 2002. In addition, we have certain diagrams that you were responsible for, so we have a lot of material. We've read that material, so we are familiar with the evidence that you are able to give the Tribunal. The purpose of having you here is so that the lawyers representing the Prosecution and the various accused can ask you questions they wish to ask, to clarify things; perhaps to add to the information to some extent, and also to challenge what you've said. To make best use of your presence, it's important to concentrate on the particular questions that counsel raise. We don't need to go over, again, the material you've given us; we already have that. So it would help us greatly if you can concentrate your mind on the particular questions and the particular issues raised in the questions, so we can get as much information as possible, as much extra information as possible from you today. The first person to ask you questions of you will be for the Prosecution, Ms. Moeller. Ms. Moeller.

utterances.speaker: MS. MOELLER
utterances.text: Thank you, Your Honours. Before I start with the witness, I would like to point out that in the witness notification we put in a footnote, saying that the 65 ter summary of the witness that was filed with pre-trial brief was incomplete, and it was lacking. Exactly, the one paragraph is evidence is mainly about, and I investigated this in the team. And there is frankly no explanation how this one paragraph could have disappeared from the version that was filed this year. This one paragraph, which is in -- which is in the 65 ter summary that we filed with the notification was, however, in the initial pre-trial brief that we filed in the original case against the three accused. And we herewith apply for leave to add back this paragraph which goes to the very heart of evidence of this witness, and I'm very embarrassed to have to do that, frankly.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE BONOMY
utterances.text: Well, I am sorry it's a problem I was not aware of. I don't see anyone leaping to their feet to give you a hard time on this, so we will grant your application.

utterances.speaker: MS. MOELLER
utterances.text: Thank you, that's appreciated very much.

utterances.speaker: MS. MOELLER
utterances.text: Good morning, Mr. Popaj. Could you please tell the Judges your full name for the record.

utterances.speaker: SABRI POPAJ
utterances.text: Sabri Popaj.

utterances.speaker: MS. MOELLER
utterances.text: And where are you from, Mr. Popaj?

utterances.speaker: SABRI POPAJ
utterances.text: I am from Bellacerka.

utterances.speaker: MS. MOELLER
utterances.text: Are you married?

utterances.speaker: SABRI POPAJ
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: MS. MOELLER
utterances.text: And do you have children?

utterances.speaker: SABRI POPAJ
utterances.text: I had two. Now I have two.

utterances.speaker: MS. MOELLER
utterances.text: Mr. Popaj, I see on the transcript it says "I had two. Now I have two." Is that correct?

utterances.speaker: SABRI POPAJ
utterances.text: Yes, that's correct.

utterances.speaker: MS. MOELLER
utterances.text: Okay.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE BONOMY
utterances.text: Well, we know that that can't be quite correct in our understanding of it. So please lead the witness to clarify that, Ms. Moeller.

utterances.speaker: MS. MOELLER
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: MS. MOELLER
utterances.text: Mr. Popaj, two of your sons died at some point in 1999, did they?

utterances.speaker: SABRI POPAJ
utterances.text: Yes, that's correct.

utterances.speaker: MS. MOELLER
utterances.text: And now you have two other sons?

utterances.speaker: SABRI POPAJ
utterances.text: One daughter and one son.

utterances.speaker: MS. MOELLER
utterances.text: And they are still alive?

utterances.speaker: SABRI POPAJ
utterances.text: Yes. One was born in the year 2000, while my son was born in 2001.

utterances.speaker: MS. MOELLER
utterances.text: Thank you. Sir, did you give a statement to the Prosecution in June 1999?

utterances.speaker: SABRI POPAJ
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: MS. MOELLER
utterances.text: And did you make some corrections in another short statement in June 2002 before you testified in the Milosevic trial?

utterances.speaker: SABRI POPAJ
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: MS. MOELLER
utterances.text: And when you came here this week, did you have the opportunity to read through your statement and the addendum statement?

utterances.speaker: SABRI POPAJ
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: MS. MOELLER
utterances.text: And when you did so, did you tell us about two changes that you wanted to notify us of, one relating to the addendum and one relating to your statement? And I will address these issues directly so you know what I'm referring to. In the addendum, did you tell us that the name of the surviving 2-year-old child was not correctly set out in the addendum?

utterances.speaker: SABRI POPAJ
utterances.text: Yes, he was from somewhere else. He was not my son; he was somebody else's son. My sons were called Shendet and Agon.

utterances.speaker: MS. MOELLER
utterances.text: Yes, I think my question was not clear. In the addendum you referred to a 2-year-old boy of the families of Zhuniqi that survived the killing of this family and you corrected his name I think. Could you tell us the correct name, his first name?

utterances.speaker: SABRI POPAJ
utterances.text: Yes, it was Zhuniqi. He was from the family of Arsim Zhuniqi and he survived.

utterances.speaker: MS. MOELLER
utterances.text: And his first name was?

utterances.speaker: SABRI POPAJ
utterances.text: Skodran Zhuniqi.

utterances.speaker: MS. MOELLER
utterances.text: Your Honours, this is the addendum. This is under additions 1.

utterances.speaker: MS. MOELLER
utterances.text: And the other aspect you pointed out to us when you read through your statement relates to the blowing up of the mosques in Celine, Bela Crkva, and Rogovo that you say.

utterances.speaker: MS. MOELLER
utterances.text: This is page 11, Your Honours.

utterances.speaker: MS. MOELLER
utterances.text: Can you explain when you explain to us, when were these three mosques blown up?

utterances.speaker: SABRI POPAJ
utterances.text: The mosques were blown up on the 28th of March, 1999.

utterances.speaker: MS. MOELLER
utterances.text: And what specific day was that?

utterances.speaker: SABRI POPAJ
utterances.text: It was Bajram.

utterances.speaker: MS. MOELLER
utterances.text: And were all three mosques blown up on the same day or on different days?

utterances.speaker: SABRI POPAJ
utterances.text: On the same day.

utterances.speaker: MS. MOELLER
utterances.text: And which one was blown up first?

utterances.speaker: SABRI POPAJ
utterances.text: The first one was the Celine one, then Bellacerka, and then I saw the Rogovo one.

utterances.speaker: MS. MOELLER
utterances.text: Thank you. Now, Mr. Popaj, with these corrections that we have now on the record, do you attest that your statements accurately reflect your evidence; and if you testified today, would you give the same account?

utterances.speaker: SABRI POPAJ
utterances.text: Yes, everything I said. Yes.

utterances.speaker: MS. MOELLER
utterances.text: Thank you.

utterances.speaker: MS. MOELLER
utterances.text: Your Honours, I would like to tender Exhibit P2446 containing both statements.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE BONOMY
utterances.text: Thank you.

utterances.speaker: MS. MOELLER
utterances.text: That's the 92 bis package. Could we call up Exhibit P93, page 6, please.

utterances.speaker: MS. MOELLER
utterances.text: Sir, I'm now calling up a picture, an aerial picture, and I would like you to point out some locations on this picture to the Honourable Judges. Can you see the picture on the screen?

utterances.speaker: SABRI POPAJ
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: MS. MOELLER
utterances.text: Okay.

utterances.speaker: MS. MOELLER
utterances.text: Could the usher assist the witness.

utterances.speaker: MS. MOELLER
utterances.text: Mr. Popaj, can you mark your houses on this picture.

utterances.speaker: SABRI POPAJ
utterances.text: Yes. My houses are here. I now live in this one. This one is also mine, this one as well, and these two here.

utterances.speaker: MS. MOELLER
utterances.text: Mm-hmm.

utterances.speaker: SABRI POPAJ
utterances.text: This is the cow-shed.

utterances.speaker: MS. MOELLER
utterances.text: Okay. And in your statement --

utterances.speaker: MS. MOELLER
utterances.text: It is page 3, Your Honours.

utterances.speaker: MS. MOELLER
utterances.text: -- you are saying that on the 25th of March five tanks entered your village. Could you make crosses where these tanks were positioned in our village that morning.

utterances.speaker: SABRI POPAJ
utterances.text: On the 25th, the tanks came from this road here. This is the road from Xerxe to Rahovec. And two got into the schoolyard, while the other three came towards the mosque, close to the mosque. It's the road that leads towards Celine, towards the hills Brestovc, Hoca e Vogel. So they were positioned here.

utterances.speaker: MS. MOELLER
utterances.text: Sir, I'm sorry, you have to mark it -- to draw it on the screen, otherwise we cannot see it. Can you make a cross where the schoolyard is that you just referred to.

utterances.speaker: SABRI POPAJ
utterances.text: Yes, I will mark it now.

utterances.speaker: MS. MOELLER
utterances.text: Okay.

utterances.speaker: SABRI POPAJ
utterances.text: [Marks]

utterances.speaker: MS. MOELLER
utterances.text: Okay. And how many tanks were there?

utterances.speaker: SABRI POPAJ
utterances.text: Two tanks were there.

utterances.speaker: MS. MOELLER
utterances.text: May the record --

utterances.speaker: JUDGE BONOMY
utterances.text: So that's the area that's circled on the right-hand side of the map.

utterances.speaker: MS. MOELLER
utterances.text: Thank you. Yes.

utterances.speaker: MS. MOELLER
utterances.text: Now, the mosque, could you also draw a line around the mosque where the other tanks were, as I understand you saying.

utterances.speaker: SABRI POPAJ
utterances.text: They did not stop at the mosque, but they moved on in this direction.

utterances.speaker: MS. MOELLER
utterances.text: Can the record reflect that on the left-hand side the witness draw a line along the street which goes above the mosque.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE BONOMY
utterances.text: Yeah.

utterances.speaker: MS. MOELLER
utterances.text: Thank you.

utterances.speaker: MS. MOELLER
utterances.text: And do you know where the tanks went to after they went your village, where they took positions?

utterances.speaker: SABRI POPAJ
utterances.text: These tanks went above the Celine village towards Nagavc, up on a hill there.

utterances.speaker: MS. MOELLER
utterances.text: And in your statement you also say that already a week before the 24th or 25th of March some troops came into your village of Bela Crkva. Which kind of uniforms, which colour of uniforms, did these troops wear?

utterances.speaker: SABRI POPAJ
utterances.text: They had light blue police uniforms and also camouflage, army, uniforms. They were positioned above the village. It was above the house of Naim Fetoshi.

utterances.speaker: MS. MOELLER
utterances.text: And the house of Naim Fetoshi, would you be able to see it on this picture or would it be outside of this --

utterances.speaker: SABRI POPAJ
utterances.text: No.

utterances.speaker: MS. MOELLER
utterances.text: That is outside of this perimeter?

utterances.speaker: SABRI POPAJ
utterances.text: Yes, you cannot see it here; it's outside this photograph.

utterances.speaker: MS. MOELLER
utterances.text: Okay. Thank you. The troops that came a week before the 24th of March, which kind of vehicles did they have, if any?

utterances.speaker: SABRI POPAJ
utterances.text: They had APCs and trucks, and they were positioned there and they began digging trenches there and they also put some -- a couple of anti-aircraft guns there. Then they took Naim Fetoshi's house. Naim Fetoshi had to leave his house with 38 members of his family. They came from their house to my house, and they were sheltered at this house here, my house.

utterances.speaker: MS. MOELLER
utterances.text: Mm-hmm. Thank you. Now, on the 25th of March, the day on which the events that we want to talk about today occurred, you went back -- you left your house, but you also went back into the village several times during that day. And you refer in your statement to seeing that houses were set on fire and that there was looting going on.

utterances.speaker: MS. MOELLER
utterances.text: This is pages 3 and 6 of the statement, Your Honours.

utterances.speaker: MS. MOELLER
utterances.text: How did the people look? What kind of clothes did they wear, who were setting the houses on fire and looting these houses?

utterances.speaker: SABRI POPAJ
utterances.text: On the 25th of March, in the morning, my family and all the people in the vicinity of the stream were leaving their houses. In the evening I returned; it was after the massacre happened in the stream of Bellacerka.

utterances.speaker: MS. MOELLER
utterances.text: Did you see any of the people who were setting the village on fire?

utterances.speaker: SABRI POPAJ
utterances.text: The village began to be set on fire in the morning, at 5.00 in the morning, on the 25th.

utterances.speaker: MS. MOELLER
utterances.text: And did the people who set the village on fire wear any uniforms; and if so, which colour uniforms?

utterances.speaker: SABRI POPAJ
utterances.text: Yes. On the 25th they had police uniforms, the ones that were setting the house on fire.

utterances.speaker: MS. MOELLER
utterances.text: And what do you mean by police uniform? What colour would they have?

utterances.speaker: SABRI POPAJ
utterances.text: It was light blue. It was not dark blue, like the army.

utterances.speaker: MS. MOELLER
utterances.text: Okay. Sir, can you, on this picture, now also show and draw a line along the Belaja River along which some of the killings occurred.

utterances.speaker: SABRI POPAJ
utterances.text: Yes, yes. The first group was from Clirim Zhuniqi's family --

utterances.speaker: MS. MOELLER
utterances.text: I'm sorry to interrupt you. Can you make a line along the Belaja river first, and we'll talk about the killings, step by step.

utterances.speaker: SABRI POPAJ
utterances.text: Yes, okay.

utterances.speaker: MS. MOELLER
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: MS. MOELLER
utterances.text: May the record reflect that the witness made a red line along the Belaja river, starting from his house going to the top of the picture.

utterances.speaker: MS. MOELLER
utterances.text: Now, sir, in your statement you refer to two families that you helped crossing this Belaja stream and were then shot. Can you indicate the location where this killing occurred, and can you put a 1, number 1, there.

utterances.speaker: SABRI POPAJ
utterances.text: [Marks]

utterances.speaker: MS. MOELLER
utterances.text: Thank you. And in your statement you also say that you observed this from a location not far away. Can you put a cross approximately where you were when you observed this shooting?

utterances.speaker: SABRI POPAJ
utterances.text: Yes. There was a pylon here, an electricity pylon, right here.

utterances.speaker: MS. MOELLER
utterances.text: And how far away was that, approximately, from the group of the two families, the Zhuniqi and the Spahiu families?

utterances.speaker: SABRI POPAJ
utterances.text: 120 metres.

utterances.speaker: MS. MOELLER
utterances.text: Thank you.

utterances.speaker: MS. MOELLER
utterances.text: May the record reflect that the cross, in the right upper corner of this photo, was the location where the witness was observing the killing of the two families from.

utterances.speaker: MS. MOELLER
utterances.text: Sir, when you saw these two families being killed, did you already use your binoculars there, or did you see it with your eyes?

utterances.speaker: SABRI POPAJ
utterances.text: I did not use the binoculars here; I saw them with my own eyes. When I left this area, this is where Halim Fetoshi was killed. And to see that I used burglars. This is where Halim Fetoshi was killed; he was born in 1932.

utterances.speaker: MS. MOELLER
utterances.text: And you saw him being killed from the same location that you saw the Spahiu and the Zhuniqi family being killed? You were in the same position then when you saw that?

utterances.speaker: SABRI POPAJ
utterances.text: Yes. Yes, the same position.

utterances.speaker: MS. MOELLER
utterances.text: Your Honours, for the clarity of the record, this particular killing is not a victim listed in Schedule B, just to make it clear.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE BONOMY
utterances.text: Is there a reason for that?

utterances.speaker: MS. MOELLER
utterances.text: No, Your Honour.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE BONOMY
utterances.text: Is it not the case that there may be other identified victims here who are not mentioned in Schedule B.

utterances.speaker: MS. MOELLER
utterances.text: Yes, indeed, all of our schedules list the ones that we were aware of at the time.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE BONOMY
utterances.text: Do you think it might be appropriate to revise these schedules, either in light of evidence that's been led or in light of evidence that may be led --

utterances.speaker: MS. MOELLER
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE BONOMY
utterances.text: -- So that we have a clear indication of the complete allegations.

utterances.speaker: MS. MOELLER
utterances.text: Yes, we will look into that, Your Honours. Thank you.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE BONOMY
utterances.text: Thank you.

utterances.speaker: MS. MOELLER
utterances.text: Now, in your statement you referred to policemen who shot these two families, which included children and women. How did these policemen look? What kind of uniform did they wear?

utterances.speaker: SABRI POPAJ
utterances.text: On my side there were 12 policemen. I don't know how many there were across the river. They had camouflage uniforms. There were others who were wearing bandannas on their heads.

utterances.speaker: MS. MOELLER
utterances.text: And the camouflage uniform, which colour camouflage was it?

utterances.speaker: SABRI POPAJ
utterances.text: It was the colour you see in the photograph, but it was lighter than this.

utterances.speaker: MS. MOELLER
utterances.text: I'm sorry, I'm not all clear. Could you say the colour.

utterances.speaker: SABRI POPAJ
utterances.text: It was green, and it was light.

utterances.speaker: MS. MOELLER
utterances.text: Okay. And just one more question regarding the colours. What colour is the curtain behind the Judges, if I may ask you? I know it sounds stupid now.

utterances.speaker: SABRI POPAJ
utterances.text: I call it green.

utterances.speaker: MS. MOELLER
utterances.text: Okay. Thank you.

utterances.speaker: MS. MOELLER
utterances.text: Your Honours, we will address that soon. It has to do with local dialects, and it occurred now for several times with several witnesses already; that there is some question about colours, and we will get an opinion from the translation service I think from the interpreters.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE BONOMY
utterances.text: Is this a suitable time to interrupt?

utterances.speaker: MS. MOELLER
utterances.text: Yes, it would be, Your Honour. Thank you.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE BONOMY
utterances.text: Mr. Popaj, we require to have a break at this time for 20 minutes. The usher will show you where you can wait while we have the break. So can you now please leave the courtroom with the usher.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE BONOMY
utterances.text: [The witness stands down].

utterances.speaker: JUDGE BONOMY
utterances.text: Ms. Moeller, I'm told that we should take a picture of this now, in case we lose it.

utterances.speaker: MS. MOELLER
utterances.text: Yes, I was just reminded by my case manager as well, Your Honour. Thank you.

utterances.speaker: THE REGISTRAR
utterances.text: That will be IC91, Your Honours.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE BONOMY
utterances.text: Thank you. We will resume at ten to 11.00.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE BONOMY
utterances.text: Ms. Moeller.

utterances.speaker: MS. MOELLER
utterances.text: Thank you. Could we call IC91 up again, please, because I would like to continue with this one. Yes. Thank you.

utterances.speaker: MS. MOELLER
utterances.text: Mr. Popaj, before we took the break, we had already talked about the shooting of the two families and the older man at the Belaja stream. Now I would like to talk with you about the killing of the big group of men that you observed. First of all, can you mark on this picture, if you can see it, where the railway track crosses the Belaja River and draw a line along there.

utterances.speaker: SABRI POPAJ
utterances.text: [Marks]

utterances.speaker: MS. MOELLER
utterances.text: Thank you.

utterances.speaker: MS. MOELLER
utterances.text: May the record reflect that the line parallel to the main street in the village, in the upper part of the photograph, reflects the railway tracks crossing the river.

utterances.speaker: MS. MOELLER
utterances.text: And the shooting of the more than 40 men that you saw that occurred at this crossing of the railway tracks and the Belaja River. Is that correct?

utterances.speaker: SABRI POPAJ
utterances.text: Yes. Exactly at the crossing.

utterances.speaker: MS. MOELLER
utterances.text: Okay. Can you put --

utterances.speaker: JUDGE BONOMY
utterances.text: Should that be 14 men?

utterances.speaker: JUDGE BONOMY
utterances.text: Thank you.

utterances.speaker: MS. MOELLER
utterances.text: Could you put a number 2 close to this crossing on this picture, please.

utterances.speaker: SABRI POPAJ
utterances.text: [Marks]

utterances.speaker: MS. MOELLER
utterances.text: Thank you. And before we talk about the details of this particular killing, I also want to ask you: After this killing, you heard further shooting. And according to your statement, later on you went to the site where you heard the shots, and you found some more bodies, bodies of six men laying at the site. Can you also indicate where this group --

utterances.speaker: MR. LUKIC
utterances.text: Your Honour.

utterances.speaker: MS. MOELLER
utterances.text: I'm sorry, Mr. Lukic is on his feet.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE BONOMY
utterances.text: Mr. Lukic.

utterances.speaker: MR. LUKIC
utterances.text: I know that we have some of these things in his statement, but our humble opinion is that when we are in a substantive area of his statement, he should be asked open questions by the Prosecutor, not to be led.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE BONOMY
utterances.text: Well, I can't say I fully understand that objection, because the witness has already said today that he testifies that this is his evidence in the statement. And all that Ms. Moeller is doing is building on a particular piece of that evidence. There doesn't seem to me to be anything wrong with that.

utterances.speaker: MR. LUKIC
utterances.text: Okay. Thank you.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE BONOMY
utterances.text: Carry on, Ms. Moeller.

utterances.speaker: MS. MOELLER
utterances.text: Your Honours, maybe I can accommodate that. I just want to have the map complete, and then I will ask some more open, specific questions about what the witness saw and heard himself.

utterances.speaker: MS. MOELLER
utterances.text: Going back to that --

utterances.speaker: MS. MOELLER
utterances.text: And it's page 4, the second-last paragraph of the witness's statement that refers to this third group of men.

utterances.speaker: MS. MOELLER
utterances.text: The area where you heard the shooting from, approximately five minutes, according to your statement, after the shooting of the bigger group of men, where did you find the six bodies, if you can put a number 3 on this photo, approximately, where the location is.

utterances.speaker: SABRI POPAJ
utterances.text: I cannot see it very well here because I went a little bit lower with the red line. But I'll put number 6 here. This photograph was taken after the year 2000; probably in 2002 or 2003.

utterances.speaker: MS. MOELLER
utterances.text: Thank you. The location that you just marked, was it along the railway tracks; and if so, in which direction, please?

utterances.speaker: SABRI POPAJ
utterances.text: No, it was on this side of the railway track. There is a water canal that goes to Celine here.

utterances.speaker: MS. MOELLER
utterances.text: And how far away, approximately, was it from the Belaja bridge where the other killing occurred, in metres, if you know?

utterances.speaker: SABRI POPAJ
utterances.text: It's 85 metres from the place where the larger group was killed; that's where the six bodies were.

utterances.speaker: MS. MOELLER
utterances.text: Thank you.

utterances.speaker: MS. MOELLER
utterances.text: May the record reflect that the site of the third killing that the witness marked is on the left-hand side, below the line that he marked as the railway tracks.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE BONOMY
utterances.text: Ms. Moeller, where, in the statement, is that reference?

utterances.speaker: MS. MOELLER
utterances.text: It is on page 4, the second-last paragraph I noted. Yes. It refers to hearing more automatic gun-fire; and then on page 7, the bottom paragraph, and page 8, the first paragraph, he sets out the names of these six men that he found there, later on.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE BONOMY
utterances.text: I'm still ...

utterances.speaker: MS. MOELLER
utterances.text: I can clarify that also with the witness, Your Honours, because I think he only heard the shooting and found the bodies later.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE BONOMY
utterances.text: No, it's the total. But I see how it's made up now. It's two of his uncle's sons plus four other people; is that right?

utterances.speaker: MS. MOELLER
utterances.text: Exactly.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE BONOMY
utterances.text: Thank you.

utterances.speaker: MS. MOELLER
utterances.text: Now I would like to go into some details about the killing of the big group of men at the Belaja bridge. When you saw the men being assembled, as you say in your statement, were you still in the location that you marked on this map, or were you somewhere else?

utterances.speaker: SABRI POPAJ
utterances.text: I was close to the railway track.

utterances.speaker: MS. MOELLER
utterances.text: So you were in the position where you just put the red dot on this mark -- on this --

utterances.speaker: SABRI POPAJ
utterances.text: Yes, the red dot.

utterances.speaker: MS. MOELLER
utterances.text: Okay. Can you make a circle around this red dot, please, just to mark it clearly.

utterances.speaker: SABRI POPAJ
utterances.text: I was about 10 metres away from the railway track.

utterances.speaker: MS. MOELLER
utterances.text: Okay. Thank you.

utterances.speaker: MS. MOELLER
utterances.text: May the record reflect that the circle in the upper right-hand corner of the picture is the position the witness was at when he saw the killing of the 40-plus men at the Belaja bridge.

utterances.speaker: MS. MOELLER
utterances.text: How far was that away from the site where the killing occurred, Mr. Popaj?

utterances.speaker: SABRI POPAJ
utterances.text: Not more than 200 metres, I would say; even less. I didn't measure the distance, but it should be around 200 metres.

utterances.speaker: MS. MOELLER
utterances.text: And while you observed the things that were going on around the Belaja bridge, did you use the binoculars that you had with you or did you only use your eyes?

utterances.speaker: SABRI POPAJ
utterances.text: I saw them through the binoculars. They were captured on the right side, past the bridge, and then they were taken on this side of the bridge.

utterances.speaker: MS. MOELLER
utterances.text: Mm-hmm.

utterances.speaker: MS. MOELLER
utterances.text: Can we take a snap-shot of this photograph, please.

utterances.speaker: THE REGISTRAR
utterances.text: That will be IC92, Your Honours.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE BONOMY
utterances.text: Thank you.

utterances.speaker: MS. MOELLER
utterances.text: And then can we call up Exhibit P93, page 2, please.

utterances.speaker: MS. MOELLER
utterances.text: While the next photograph is coming up, I would like to ask you to clarify something for the Honourable Judges and for us here in the courtroom. In your statement --

utterances.speaker: MS. MOELLER
utterances.text: This is page 4 of the statement, Your Honours.

utterances.speaker: MS. MOELLER
utterances.text: -- you say that you recognised your oldest son, Shendet, being in this group of men that was assembled at the Belaja bridge, but that you only learned later from your wife and your parents that your other son, your two brothers, and your nephew were in the same group. What I would like to clarify with you is what could you actually see, and why could you see Shendet but not the others? If you could explain that to the Judges, please.

utterances.speaker: SABRI POPAJ
utterances.text: I saw through the binoculars, when they were brought from this side to this side here. And here, at the telephone pylon/pole, they were assembled there. I was on the other side. When they made them take off their clothes, searched them, and plundered them, they took them then here. And when they executed them, Shendet was here, at this location, and my brother Nesim, while the others were down here.

utterances.speaker: MS. MOELLER
utterances.text: Okay. Can you mark with the pen, if the usher could assist, the way that the group that you just explained walked, just as you showed now with the indications, that we have it on the --

utterances.speaker: SABRI POPAJ
utterances.text: They stopped them here and they were all turned with their faces towards the river.

utterances.speaker: MS. MOELLER
utterances.text: Can you make a cross where you just ended the line, please.

utterances.speaker: SABRI POPAJ
utterances.text: [Marks]

utterances.speaker: MS. MOELLER
utterances.text: So at this location, the group was assembled, you said, and they were searched?

utterances.speaker: SABRI POPAJ
utterances.text: They searched them. They had them -- their coats removed, searched their coats, and took everything that they had in their coats.

utterances.speaker: MS. MOELLER
